title: CC spend YoY — ecommerce 32.2% vs in-store POS 23.4%
body: On a year-on-year basis, credit card ecommerce transaction volume grew 32.2% and in-store POS volume grew 23.4% as of Aug 2026. Year-on-year removes the heavy seasonality in the monthly numbers — online is outpacing in-store on a clean comparison.
implication: Credit card spend is growing across both channels year-on-year (ecom faster). A spend mix tilting online is a mix of more card-not-present volume, where fraud and dispute rates run higher — so the channel mix carries risk information the headline spend growth does not.

chain: CC ecommerce volume up 32.2% YoY vs POS up 23.4% YoY — both growing, seasonally clean
Online (CNP) is the faster-growing channel on a year-on-year basis
Channel mix shift changes the fraud and dispute profile — risk models must track mix, not just total spend

title: Gap: Foreign bank CC share at 3.4% (-0.0pp MoM) — premium segment shrinking
body: Foreign banks hold only 3.4% of total credit cards outstanding in Aug 2026, down 0.03pp vs prior month. Foreign banks traditionally serve the high-income, high-spend segment — their declining share signals continued loss of the premium CC market to private Indian banks.
implication: Foreign banks (Amex, Standard Chartered, etc.) traditionally served high-income customers — high credit limits, frequent international travel, premium cards. With their share at just 3.4% and still falling, those customers are now largely being served by Indian private banks instead. For anyone analysing RBI's credit card data, this means the premium borrower segment is now in the domestic bank numbers — not in a separate foreign bank bucket.

title: PSB banks hold 63.6% of debit cards — Payments gaining share in Aug 2026
body: Public sector banks account for 63.6% of total debit cards outstanding in Aug 2026 (-0.1pp vs prior month). Private banks hold 25.9%. Payments banks are the fastest-growing category (+0.1pp share gain).
implication: PSBs (government-owned banks like SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda) hold 63.6% of debit cards, largely because of Jan Dhan — the government scheme that opened basic bank accounts for millions of low-income households. Many of these accounts have little activity. If you're using debit transaction data for credit assessment, PSB debit data needs to be treated very differently from, say, HDFC or Kotak debit customers.

title: Gap: DC ATM cash at 79.9% of DC volume — digital transition is incomplete
body: Despite growth in digital payments, ATM cash withdrawals still account for 79.9% of total debit card transaction volume in Aug 2026 (-0.1pp vs prior month). DC ecommerce is only 5.4% of DC volume. India's debit card base remains overwhelmingly cash-dependent.
implication: 79.9% of debit card spending is ATM cash. Cash leaves no digital record — you can't tell where it was spent or on what. For lenders trying to assess a debit card holder's financial behaviour, the transaction history is mostly blank. Bureau scores (CIBIL, Experian) remain the primary tool for this segment — debit transaction data alone isn't enough yet.

title: Gap: Offsite ATMs declining -0.2% MoM — rural cash access contracting
body: Offsite ATMs fell 0.2% MoM in Aug 2026 (now 73,298), while onsite ATMs grew +0.3% MoM. Offsite ATMs serve rural and semi-urban populations where branch presence is limited — their decline reduces physical cash access for underserved geographies.
implication: Offsite ATMs are standalone machines in villages, petrol pumps, small towns — placed away from bank branches specifically to serve rural areas. When these decline and digital payments haven't reached those areas yet, rural borrowers lose their easiest way to access cash for repayment. If you have loans in rural geographies, check whether ATM coverage in those areas is shrinking — it can make EMI collection harder.

title: Private Sector Banks took 67.0% of all new credit cards in the past year
body: Of the credit cards added over the past twelve months, Private Sector Banks took 67.0% — the largest share of the new money — growing 9.7% a year and slowing (-0.11 pp). The rest went to Public Sector Banks 23.9%; Small Finance Banks 11.5%; Foreign Banks -2.3%.
implication: Shares of new lending move far faster than shares of the book, so this is the earlier read of the two. It says where the money went, not why — and a falling share alongside rising growth means the others grew faster, not that this one shrank.

title: Payment Banks shed ground to Public Sector Banks — the net barely moved
body: Debit cards shows almost no net change over the year, but a great deal happened underneath it: Public Sector Banks expanded while Payment Banks contracted by a similar amount. Public Sector Banks accounts for 31.4% of the total movement and Payment Banks for -28.5%. Almost none of that movement survives into the net figure — this period is a transfer between members, not a change in size.
implication: The headline number is the least informative part of this period. The reallocation between members is the finding.

title: Credit cards in force grew faster than credit card spend (+4.41 pp apart over a year)
body: Credit cards in force and credit card spend normally move together — they are two readings of the same activity. Over the past year they have come apart. Both grew over the year, credit cards in force the faster of the two. Measured as credit cards in force minus credit card spend, the two year-on-year rates are +4.41 pp apart. At the bank level the gap is concentrated, not general: 2 banks are flagged — CSB BANK LTD. +17.98 pp; ICICI BANK LTD +15.36 pp.
implication: A gap between credit cards in force and credit card spend is a question, not a conclusion: the two sides can part company because behaviour changed, because one side has a base effect, or because reporting shifted. Watch whether the gap closes next month — a pair that stays apart for several months is telling you the relationship itself has changed.

chain: Credit cards in force and credit card spend are a declared pair: each side's growth is measured against the same month a year earlier.
Both grew over the year, credit cards in force the faster of the two.
The gap between the two rates — credit cards in force minus credit card spend — is +4.41 pp, wide enough to count as a divergence rather than ordinary drift.
2 banks show the same split on their own books, the widest at +17.98 pp.
